summary: Introduces a well-known localEngineID and a discovery mechanism that lets an SNMPv3 application learn the snmpEngineID of a remote SNMP engine. SNMPv3 needs that identifier before it can retrieve or manage objects on a remote entity. It updates RFC 3411 and has Internet Standard status.

plainLanguage.summary: Before talking to a device you need to know its name tag. This gives a way to ask any SNMP device what its name tag is, so you can start the conversation.

questions: how to find remote snmp engine id
how to discover snmpv3 engine id
what is a snmp context engine id
subtitle: A well-known placeholder engine ID that lets an SNMPv3 application ask a device for its real snmpEngineID.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 needs the remote engine's snmpEngineID to read or change managed objects, and not every security model can discover it.
tldr.mechanism: A well-known localEngineID value (80 00 00 00 06 in hex) always refers to the local default context, so a manager can use it to read the real snmpEngineID.0 scalar.
tldr.outcome: A manager can learn the remote engine ID independently of the security model. The RFC is an Internet Standard and updates RFC 3411.

today: RFC 5343 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3411.

sections.title: The Problem: Finding the Engine ID
sections.content:
To retrieve or manage information with SNMPv3, you need to know the identifier of the remote SNMP engine, the snmpEngineID. It can be configured by hand on each management application for each agent, but it is often better to discover it automatically.

This RFC introduces a discovery mechanism that is independent of the features of SNMP security models. It is designed to coexist with discovery built into security models, such as the authoritative engine identifier discovery of the User-based Security Model (USM). It also updates RFC 3411 by clarifying the IANA rules for the SnmpEngineID format registry.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot send a letter to a device without knowing its name. You could write the name down by hand, but it is nicer if you can just ask.

sections.title: Contexts and Context Engine IDs
sections.content:
An SNMP engine is uniquely identified within an administrative domain by its snmpEngineID. An SNMP context is a collection of management information accessible by an SNMP entity. A context is identified by a contextEngineID (the snmpEngineID of the entity hosting the information) and a contextName.

An individual item of management information is identified by a four-tuple: contextEngineID, contextName, object type and instance identification. SNMPv3 messages carry a scopedPDU, which holds a contextEngineID, a contextName and a PDU.

Context engine IDs act as end-to-end identifiers, which matters with SNMP proxies. Engine IDs also separate the identity of an engine from the transport addresses used to reach it, so information can be correlated even when different transports are used or addresses change.

To read data from an SNMPv3 agent you must know the right contextEngineID. USM can discover the snmpEngineID because it needs it for security processing. Other security models, such as the Transport Security Model (TSM), lack this and may use the mechanism of this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Every device has a name tag, and the thing you want to ask about lives in a named folder on that device. To ask, you need both the device's name tag and the folder name.

sections.title: The Well-Known localEngineID
sections.content:
The mechanism has two parts. The first is a special well-known snmpEngineID called the localEngineID, which always refers to the local default context. The second is a procedure for reading the snmpEngineID scalar of the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB using that value.

A command responder implementing this RFC MUST register its pduTypes under the localEngineID by calling registerContextEngineID(), in addition to its normal registration under its own snmpEngineID. The value uses the variable-length format 3 of the SnmpEngineID textual convention, allocating the previously reserved format value 6 with enterprise ID 0: '8000000006'H.

The localEngineID is only a special value for the contextEngineID field of a ScopedPDU. It MUST NOT be used to identify an engine, so it MUST NOT appear in the snmpEngineID.0 scalar or in the msgAuthoritativeEngineID field of USM security parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a magic word that means "the device I am talking to, whatever its name is." You only use it when asking, never as the device's real name.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
Discovery sends a Read Class operation for the snmpEngineID scalar, using the localEngineID as the contextEngineID. Implementations SHOULD only do this when needed. If the security model already discovers the remote snmpEngineID (such as USM), or the application already knows a suitable value, no further discovery is necessary.

The procedure is: (1) if a suitable contextEngineID is already known, use it and stop; (2) if the security model supports discovery, let it discover the snmpEngineID, assign it to the contextEngineID and stop; (3) send a Read Class operation with the localEngineID as contextEngineID to retrieve snmpEngineID.0 of the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB, and on success use the retrieved value; (4) otherwise return an error that no suitable contextEngineID could be discovered.

The RFC calls this procedure an example. Step 3 can be modified to retrieve more variables, such as the sysObjectID.0 or snmpSetSerialNo.0 scalars of the SNMPv2-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: First check if you already know the name. If not, see if the security system can tell you. If not, use the magic word and ask. If that fails, give up and say so.

sections.title: The SnmpEngineID Format Registry
sections.content:
RFC 3411 asked IANA to create a registry of SnmpEngineID formats but did not record the initial assignments or spell out allocation rules. This RFC sets the rules. The first four octets of an SnmpEngineID carry an enterprise number, and the fifth octet, the format octet, says how the rest is formed.

The existing values are 0 (reserved), 1 (IPv4 address), 2 (IPv6 address), 3 (MAC address), 4 (administratively assigned text), 5 (administratively assigned octets), 6 to 127 (reserved) and 128 to 255 (enterprise specific). IANA can assign new values out of 1 to 127, and a specification is required as per RFC 5226. The range 128 to 255 is not controlled by IANA. Per this RFC, IANA assigned format 6, "local engine".
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of the kinds of name tags a device can have. This RFC writes down the rules for adding to the list and adds one new entry, the magic word.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends using the security services of SNMPv3, and in particular RECOMMENDS protecting the discovery exchange. An snmpEngineID can contain a device's MAC address, IPv4 address, IPv6 address or administratively assigned text, so an attacker behind a router, firewall or NAT might discover engine IDs to learn that information.

Even so, in many environments making the engine ID readable at security level noAuthNoPriv helps legitimate tools, which is why the default VACM configuration in RFC 3415 gives noAuthNoPriv read access to it. The USM discovery mechanism of RFC 3414 also uses unprotected messages and reveals engine IDs. In highly secure environments, engine IDs can be protected by using this discovery together with a security model that does not exchange cleartext messages, such as TSM.

The access control subsystem does not consider the contextEngineID when checking access rights, so a special view for discovery cannot be defined. A request with the localEngineID is treated like one with the correct snmpEngineID.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag can give away facts about a device, like its address. Most of the time that is fine, but in very careful setups you should ask in a private, scrambled way.
